parts.title: Men with more body fat tended to have lower testosterone
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Background

Testosterone is a hormone, a chemical messenger made mostly in the testes. In men, lower levels of testosterone have again and again been linked to problems with how the body handles food and energy, especially obesity. In this study, we wanted to understand how testosterone and obesity are connected. To do this, we looked at how testosterone levels line up with body fat percentage, which is the share of a person's body weight made up of fat. We used data from NHANES (the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey), a large national health survey in the United States.

Methods

We studied 5959 people who took part in NHANES from 2011 to 2016. We used a statistical method called multivariable linear regression. It estimates how much one measurement changes, on average, when another goes up by one unit, while taking other factors into account at the same time. With it, we looked at how testosterone was linked to five measures of body makeup:

- total percent fat (TPF): the share of the body that is fat overall
- android percent fat (APF): fat in the belly and lower trunk
- gynoid percent fat (GPF): fat in the hips and thighs
- the android to gynoid ratio (A/G): belly fat compared with hip and thigh fat
- lean mass percent (LMP): the share of the body that is muscle and other non-fat tissue

We also ran the same analysis separately for men and for women. Sometimes the link between two measurements is not a straight line. To allow for this, we also drew smooth curves through the data and used a method called generalized additive models, which can follow curved patterns. Finally, we repeated the analysis only for people with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or more, to check whether our conclusions held up. BMI (body mass index) is a measure of weight compared with height.

Result

In men, testosterone levels showed a statistically significant negative link with TPF (β = -11.97, P <0.0001), APF (β = -9.36, P<0.0001), GPF (β = -10.29, P <0.0001) and A/G (β = -320.93, P<0.0001). In other words, men with more of these kinds of fat tended to have lower testosterone. The β value tells how much testosterone changes for each one-unit rise in a body measure. A negative β means testosterone goes down as the measure goes up. LMP showed the opposite, a positive link with testosterone (β = 12.62, P<0.0001): men with a larger share of lean mass tended to have higher testosterone.

In women, the pattern between testosterone and body fat was the reverse. However, in women with obesity, we found no statistically significant link between testosterone and body makeup. This means we could not show a link in that group, though it does not prove there is none.

Conclusions

Our findings support a negative link between body fat and testosterone levels in men.
parts.introduction_first: Obesity is a disease of the body's energy use, in which a person has too much fat tissue. It is defined as a BMI (body mass index) of 30 kg/m2 or more. BMI is a measure of weight compared with height. Around the world, obesity has become much more common. Along with it, many health problems have become more common too, such as heart and blood vessel disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, problems with muscles and bones, breathing diseases, and certain cancers [1]. These diseases can leave people unable to do everyday things and can cause early death. They can also make life much harder and shorten how long people live. In recent years, scientists have become very interested in how obesity is connected to hypogonadism, a condition in which the body does not make enough of its sex hormones. Many studies have reported that testosterone, a male sex hormone, plays different roles in obesity in men and in women.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

To sum up, our results showed that men with lower testosterone levels tend to have a larger share of fat in their bodies and a smaller share of lean mass. In women, by contrast, we found no statistically significant link between testosterone and body makeup. Why men and women show these different patterns still needs more research.
parts.introduction_rest:
Testosterone is one of the most important members of the androgens, the family of hormones that includes male sex hormones. Most of it is made in the testes. In women, smaller amounts are made in the ovaries and in the adrenal glands, small glands that sit on top of the kidneys. Testosterone can work together with estrogen, a female sex hormone, to help control how the reproductive organs of men and women develop and work. It also plays an important part in other organs of the body. By controlling how the body handles protein and fat, testosterone can affect the quality of muscles, where fat is stored, and how the body uses energy [2].

In men, not having enough testosterone can lead to more fat being stored and made, and to fat cells multiplying. It can also lead to less muscle in the arms and legs and a lower basal metabolic rate, which is the number of calories the body burns at rest. Together, these changes can make weight gain worse, raise body fat percentage, and add to metabolic syndrome, a group of problems such as high blood sugar and high blood pressure that often appear together. They can also cause other health problems [3–5].

However, these studies have been limited by small sample sizes. When only a few people are studied, the results may not apply to everyone, and the study may be less able to detect a link even if one exists. So in this study, we set out to look at how testosterone levels are connected to obesity, using a large set of data from NHANES (the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey). In particular, we wanted to see how testosterone affects body makeup in both men and women. To measure body makeup, we used DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry), a scan that uses two kinds of X-rays to measure how much fat, muscle and bone a person has. Our results may help people better understand the part testosterone plays in obesity and the health risks that come with it. They may also be important for developing good ways to manage obesity.
parts.methods:
Materials and methods

Who we studied

Our data came from NHANES (the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey), a large national health survey in the United States. It was run by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) between 2011 and 2016. Fig 1 shows how we chose who was included and who was left out.

We started with 21,592 people who had complete testosterone data. We then left out 8,686 people whose body makeup data were incomplete. We also left out 4,091 people who were under 18, and 2,856 people who had taken medicines known to possibly change testosterone levels, such as birth control pills, estrogen and aldactone. That left 5959 people aged 18 to 59 who had complete data and had had a DXA scan. A DXA scan is a quick X-ray scan that measures how much fat and how much lean mass (muscle and other non-fat tissue) are in different parts of the body.

The National Center for Health Statistics Research Ethics Review Board carefully reviewed the NHANES study and its methods and approved them. Before taking part, every person freely gave their informed consent by signing a consent form. This means they agreed to take part after being told what the study involved. The particular round of NHANES that we used is a continuation of Protocol #2011–17. More details are on the CDC website: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/irba98.htm.

Fig 1

How we chose the people in our study from NHANES 2011–2016.

What we measured

We looked at five measures of body makeup. These were total percent fat (TPF), the share of the body that is fat overall; android percent fat (APF), the share of fat in the belly and lower trunk; gynoid percent fat (GPF), the share of fat in the hips and thighs; the android to gynoid ratio (A/G), belly fat compared with hip and thigh fat; and lean mass percent (LMP), the share of the body that is muscle and other non-fat tissue.

All of these were measured with Hologic Discovery model A densitometers (Hologic, Inc., Bedford, Massachusetts), a type of DXA scanner, using software version Apex 3.2. Trained and certified radiology technologists took the scans.

To work out TPF, we divided total fat mass by total fat and lean mass. To measure belly fat, the scanner marked out the lower trunk. It used two lines: a horizontal line across the lower pelvis, and a second line that the software placed automatically above it. For hip and thigh fat, the upper line sat 1.5 times the height of the belly region below the pelvic line. The lower line was placed so that the distance between the two hip-and-thigh lines was twice the height of the belly region [6]. We then divided APF by GPF to get the A/G ratio. Finally, we divided total lean mass by the total of fat and lean mass to get LMP. The Hologic software placed all of these lines automatically.

Testosterone was the outcome we were trying to explain. It was measured with a lab method called isotope dilution liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (ID-LC-MS/MS). This method separates the chemicals in a blood sample and then identifies and measures each one by its weight. The CDC regularly developed this method. Details of the testosterone measurements are in the Laboratory Data section of the survey reports: the Sex Steroid Hormone chapter for the 2013–2014 and 2015–2016 rounds, and the Total Testosterone chapter for the 2011–2012 round.

We also took other factors into account. These included people's age, gender, ethnicity and BMI (body mass index, a measure of weight compared with height). We also included family income compared with the poverty level, which shows how much a family earns compared with the amount needed to get by. We measured the distance around the arm and around the waist.

We also included whether people had high blood pressure, high cholesterol or diabetes. We counted someone as a smoker if they had smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime. We included whether they did hard physical work, and several blood test results: cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen and uric acid. These are all substances in the blood that can give clues about a person's health. More details about all of these factors are on the official NHANES website.

How we analyzed the data

We described the people in our study in a few ways. For measurements that follow a normal distribution, a bell-shaped spread where most values sit near the middle, we gave the average (mean) and the standard deviation (SD), which shows how spread out the values are. For measurements that did not follow this pattern, we gave the median, the middle value, along with the first and third quartiles (Q1 and Q3), the values a quarter and three-quarters of the way up the list. For things that fall into categories, such as whether someone had diabetes, we gave percentages.

To find the link between body makeup and testosterone, we used multivariable linear regression. This method estimates how much one measurement changes, on average, when another goes up by one unit, while taking other factors into account at the same time. We built three versions of the model. Model 1 took no other factors into account. Model 2 took age, sex and race into account. Model 3 built on Model 2 and also took high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking and hard physical work into account. We also ran the analysis separately for men and for women.

The link between body makeup and testosterone might not be a straight line. To allow for this, we drew smooth curves through the data and used generalized additive models, a method that can follow curved patterns. We did all of our analyses with the computer programs R (http://www.Rproject.org) and EmpowerStats (http://www.empowerstats.com). We called a result statistically significant when P was below 0.05. This means that if there were really no link, a result this strong would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.
parts.results:
Results

In total, 5959 people with complete information were included in this study. Table 1 describes the men and the women in our study. Because NHANES surveys some groups of people more often than others, we used weights so that each group counts fairly in the picture of the whole population.

Men and women differed in several ways at the start of the study. First, men had much higher testosterone levels than women, and this difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For p < 0.001, that would happen less than 0.1% of the time.

Men took in more energy overall, and more protein, carbohydrates and fat, than women. Even so, they had a smaller share of total body fat, belly fat and hip and thigh fat than women did. Men also had a higher A/G ratio, a larger share of lean mass, and bigger arms and waists. All of these differences had p-values below 0.001. Men also had a lower BMI than women (p < 0.01).

Women were less likely than men to have high blood pressure, high blood fat levels (hyperlipidemia), to smoke, or to do vigorous physical activity. The share of people with diabetes was about the same in both groups, and the difference was not statistically significant.

How body makeup is linked to testosterone

In our main analysis (model 3), we took into account age, sex, race, high blood pressure, diabetes, high blood fat levels, smoking and vigorous work activity. After this, we found statistically significant negative links between testosterone and total body fat, belly fat, hip and thigh fat, and the A/G ratio. In other words, people with more of these kinds of fat tended to have lower testosterone. Lean mass showed the opposite, a statistically significant positive link with testosterone.

When we ran the analysis separately for men and women, men showed the same pattern. Women showed the reverse: in women, higher testosterone went along with a larger share of body fat and a smaller share of lean mass. Table 2 gives the full results.

For each 1% rise in lean mass, testosterone rose by 12.62 ng/dL.

In women, the pattern was the reverse. Testosterone went up with total body fat, belly fat, hip and thigh fat and the A/G ratio, and it went down with the share of lean mass. For each 1% rise in total body fat, testosterone rose by 0.19 ng/dL. For each 1% rise in belly fat, it rose by 0.15 ng/dL, while for each 1% rise in hip and thigh fat, it fell by 0.15 ng/dL. For each one-unit rise in the A/G ratio, testosterone rose by 7.83 ng/dL. For each 1% rise in lean mass, testosterone fell by 0.21 ng/dL.

parts.discussion:
Discussion

Our study showed clear differences between men and women in how much energy they took in and in their body makeup. Men took in more energy overall than women. At the same time, men had less total percent fat (TPF), less fat in the belly and lower trunk (APF), less fat in the hips and thighs (GPF), and a lower BMI. Men also had a higher A/G ratio, a larger share of lean mass (LMP), and bigger arms and waists than women.

When we looked more closely, we found that in men, higher testosterone went along with less total percent fat, less belly fat and less hip and thigh fat. Higher testosterone also went along with more lean body mass (LBM), the weight of the body that is not fat. In women, however, we found no statistically significant link between testosterone and body makeup. These results suggest that testosterone may affect the bodies of men and women in different ways.

In men, testosterone is known to play a key part in controlling metabolism, the way the body uses food and energy. Studies have shown that low testosterone levels may lead to obesity. In patients with prostate cancer, a treatment that removes the body's testosterone can increase the fat stored around the organs inside the belly, the fat just under the skin of the belly, and the total amount of fat [7]. On the other hand, giving extra testosterone to men with low testosterone and a large waist has been shown to reduce the fat under the skin of the belly and the thighs [8]. In young men, weight loss and bariatric surgery (surgery to help people lose weight) have also been linked to higher levels of total testosterone and of free testosterone, the part of testosterone that is not attached to other substances in the blood [9]. Together, these findings suggest that in men, testosterone and obesity may affect each other in both directions.

Obesity may cause hypogonadism in men. In people with obesity, fat cells contain more of an enzyme called aromatase. This enzyme turns testosterone into estradiol, a form of estrogen [10]. Estradiol, along with other signals made by fat cells such as TNF, IL-6 and leptin, can reduce how much testosterone the body makes in several ways. These include blocking the chain of signals that runs from the brain to the testes (the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis) [11], weakening the work of nerve cells that make a signal called kisspeptin [12], and leptin directly blocking the release of hormones that tell the testes to work [13]. The link can also run the other way. A lack of testosterone can push stem cells, which can turn into many kinds of cells, to become fat cells, and this may make obesity worse [14].

On the other hand, giving men extra testosterone can help burn fat. It does this by making fat cells produce more of the receptors that respond to norepinephrine, a chemical messenger that helps the body break down fat [15]. It can also stop fat from being stored by making an enzyme called LPL, which helps take fat into fat cells, work less on the surface of those cells [16]. In addition, testosterone can lower the amount of a protein called PPARγ in preadipocytes, the early cells that can become fat cells, and this stops them from turning into fat cells [14]. Studies have also shown that extra testosterone can increase the breakdown of fat and raise signs of activity in the mitochondria, the tiny power stations inside cells, in fat tissue. This points to fat cells possibly using energy faster [17].

Men also need enough testosterone to keep their muscle mass, and a lack of testosterone may lead to losing muscle. In patients with prostate cancer who received GnRHa treatment, a medicine that blocks the signals to the testes, for 48 weeks, the share of their body that was muscle fell by 2.7%. Arik Davidyan and colleagues studied how testosterone affects muscle mass. They found that muscle mass fell significantly in mice whose testes had been removed [18].

Giving men extra testosterone increases muscle mass and strength. Several studies have reported that testosterone treatment increases lean body mass in men, with gains ranging from 1.9 kg to 3.6 kg [19–21], depending on how long the treatment lasts and how much testosterone is given. Testosterone treatment has also been shown to improve how well muscles work and how well people walk [21]. Testosterone makes muscles grow by making two kinds of muscle fibers, type I and type II, get bigger. It also increases the number of muscle bundles and of satellite cells, which are stem cells that help repair and build muscle [22].

In women, the link between testosterone levels and body makeup is still unclear. Some studies suggest that women with higher testosterone have more body fat [23, 24], while others find no clear link between the two [25, 26]. This suggests that the link is complicated and may depend on things such as BMI, age and the balance of hormones in the body.

Some women have unusually high levels of androgens, the group of hormones that includes testosterone. One example is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a common hormone condition in women. Women with PCOS often have overweight or obesity, which is linked to insulin resistance (the body not responding properly to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar) and to other problems with metabolism [27]. In women with PCOS, the enzymes that convert one sex hormone into another are more active. This shows that these sex hormones affect how fat tissue works at the level of the tissue itself. Even so, the link between obesity and high androgen levels in women with PCOS is not yet fully settled. In most studies of women with PCOS, higher total testosterone went along with having belly fat and with having more of it [28, 29]. But some studies found no link between fat build-up and total testosterone [30].

The complicated link between testosterone levels and where fat is stored in women is still unclear. The main reason is that studies of how this works have not shown a clear difference between men and women in how testosterone controls fat. For example, testosterone can stop cells from becoming fat cells, help fat cells break down fat, and help the body process fat [31]. In addition, some studies have shown that giving women a suitable amount of extra testosterone plays an important part in keeping their metabolism working well. Davis and colleagues found that testosterone replacement therapy, which gives women extra testosterone, improved body makeup in women with low testosterone, including lowering body fat and increasing muscle mass [32]. Liang and colleagues found that adult women with higher total testosterone had a gradually lower risk of metabolic syndrome, a group of problems that includes high blood sugar, high blood pressure and extra belly fat [33].

Our results therefore help us understand better how testosterone is linked to where fat is stored in the body. They also point the way for further research on how testosterone levels and body makeup in women are connected in diseases linked to high androgens, such as PCOS and hyperandrogenism (having too much of these hormones).
